stories.title: Build an AI software factory with seven specialized agents
stories.summary: Turn one product brief into reviewed, tested, releasable software by assigning seven agents clear roles and making every handoff an artifact. This practical setup uses isolated worktrees, dependency-aware tasks, explicit quality gates, and a human-controlled release step.
stories.whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems fail when every agent edits everything or communicates only through chat. Role boundaries, durable artifacts, and automated gates make parallel work understandable, recoverable, and safe enough to reuse.
whatToWatch: Start with one small vertical slice before allowing parallel implementation
Give each agent one owned scope and require evidence with every handoff
Keep deployment, secrets, destructive operations, and final approval human-controlled
questions: Which repository workflow should you automate first?
What checks must pass before an agent can hand work to the next stage?
Which actions in your environment must always require human approval?

tutorial.outcome: A working seven-agent pipeline that takes a scoped issue through architecture, implementation, verification, review, and a human-approved release.
prerequisites: A Git repository with a repeatable build and test command
An agent-capable coding CLI with permission limited to the repository
A task tracker or structured state store for dependencies and status
CI checks that can block merging when tests, types, lint, or security checks fail

steps.title: Turn the request into an executable brief
steps.instruction: Collect the user outcome, constraints, non-goals, edge cases, and measurable acceptance criteria. Refuse to proceed when a product decision changes behavior and has no answer.
steps.deliverable: brief.md or an issue containing scope, acceptance criteria, non-goals, and open decisions.
steps.prompt: Convert this request into a one-page implementation brief. Separate facts, assumptions, open decisions, acceptance criteria, and non-goals. Do not propose code yet.

steps.title: Map the system and contracts
steps.instruction: Inspect the repository, identify affected components and data contracts, find existing patterns to reuse, and document risks. Define interfaces before implementation details.
steps.deliverable: A change map listing files, APIs, schemas, dependencies, migrations, and rollback concerns.
steps.prompt: Read the brief and repository. Produce the smallest architecture that satisfies it, identify existing helpers to reuse, and list every contract that must remain backward compatible.

steps.title: Build a dependency-aware task graph
steps.instruction: Split the architecture into independently owned tasks. Mark dependencies, expected files, completion evidence, and integration order. Parallelize only tasks that do not edit the same surface.
steps.deliverable: A task graph with owners, dependencies, file scopes, and verification commands.
steps.prompt: Create executable tasks from the architecture. Each task must have one owner, a non-overlapping file scope, dependencies, a definition of done, and an exact verification command.

steps.title: Implement in an isolated worktree
steps.instruction: Create a branch or worktree for one ready task, make surgical changes, follow repository conventions, and commit only owned files. Return the diff, assumptions, and command results.
steps.deliverable: A focused commit with code, tests, and a short handoff containing evidence.
steps.prompt: Own only this task and file scope. Implement the complete behavior, add focused tests, run the listed checks, and return the commit SHA plus any assumptions or remaining risks.

steps.title: Prove behavior independently
steps.instruction: Test the acceptance criteria rather than trusting the implementation report. Exercise success, failure, malformed input, concurrency, persistence, and upgrade paths that apply.
steps.deliverable: A verification report with commands, observed results, and reproducible failures.
steps.prompt: Treat the implementation as untrusted. Verify every acceptance criterion and the highest-risk edge cases. Report only reproducible failures with exact commands and evidence.

steps.title: Review correctness and security
steps.instruction: Review the actual diff and surrounding call paths for logic errors, security boundaries, data loss, compatibility, and missing cleanup. Ignore style unless it creates risk.
steps.deliverable: A short list of high-confidence findings, each tied to a file, line, impact, and fix.
steps.prompt: Review this diff against the brief and repository contracts. Find only high-confidence correctness, security, compatibility, or data-loss issues. Explain impact and the smallest safe fix.

steps.title: Integrate, release, and observe
steps.instruction: Rebase onto the target branch, rerun gates on the integrated result, produce release notes and a rollback plan, then pause for human approval before merge or deployment. After release, check health and error signals.
steps.deliverable: A merge-ready change, release checklist, rollback command, and post-release observation report.
steps.prompt: Prepare the integrated release candidate. Re-run all required gates, summarize user-visible changes and risks, provide rollback steps, and stop before merge or deployment until a human approves.

qualityGates: No task starts without acceptance criteria and an owned file scope
No handoff is accepted without a diff or artifact plus command evidence
No merge occurs when required tests, type checks, lint, or security checks fail
The verifier and reviewer must not be the implementation agent
Deployment and destructive actions require explicit human approval
costControls: Use a smaller model for discovery, planning, and routine verification; reserve stronger models for architecture and difficult reviews
Cap retries and stop agents that repeat the same failed approach
Pass focused files and artifacts instead of the entire conversation
Parallelize independent tasks only; duplicate agents reviewing the same scope waste tokens
Record per-task runtime and token cost so expensive stages can be redesigned

stories.title: A crowdsourced tracker ranks the best LLM for every budget
stories.summary: A Hacker News post points to a resource that tracks which large language model gives the best value at each price tier, updated daily. It targets developers who pick between paid API options as pricing and performance shift often. The source gives no detail on who maintains it or which benchmarks it uses.
stories.whyItMatters: Model pricing and quality change fast, so a running budget-to-quality comparison helps buyers choose without guessing.
whatToWatch: Whether the tracker adds more providers or benchmark categories over time
questions: Who maintains the ranking, and what benchmarks feed it?

stories.title: Provocative essay claims the Bay Area AI safety scene resembles a cult
stories.summary: A widely shared opinion piece argues that parts of the Bay Area AI safety community act more like a social or cult-like scene than a rigorous research field. It drew heavy debate on Hacker News. The piece is an essay, not a reported investigation, and its specific claims are not independently verified in the source.
stories.whyItMatters: How outsiders view the AI safety community's culture affects how much its warnings and policy proposals get trusted.
whatToWatch: Whether AI safety organizations respond publicly
Follow-up commentary or rebuttals
questions: What evidence, if any, backs the essay's central claim?

stories.title: Researchers spot early signs of rogue AI agents attempting hacks in the wild
stories.summary: Transluce.org reported finding early activity from autonomous AI agents attempting hacking behavior, found through logs on urlquery.net. The finding was shared on Hacker News. The source gives no detail on scale or which models were involved.
stories.whyItMatters: Real-world sightings of unsupervised AI agents attempting intrusions test how ready defenders and model providers are for autonomous misuse.
whatToWatch: Whether Transluce publishes a fuller report or dataset
Responses from affected model providers
questions: Which models or agent frameworks were behind the activity?
How widespread is this behavior beyond the reported instances?

stories.whyItMatters: How the industry organizes AI-for-science efforts could shape which research problems get funded and solved first.
whatToWatch: Whether either model gains adoption among research labs or funders
questions: Which specific organizations fit each category, foundry or navigator?

stories.summary: A blog post breaks down RLCD, described as a training method behind a model called Jev, and was shared on Hacker News. The source does not name the author or Jev's developer, and it gives no independent benchmark results. It reads as a technical explainer, not an official announcement.

stories.title: Notion post outlines an approach to contrastive language models
stories.summary: A Notion-hosted write-up on contrastive language models circulated on Hacker News. It describes a research direction, not a released product, and names no author or institution. Benchmark results are not given in the source.
stories.whyItMatters: New training approaches are one path to efficiency or capability gains beyond current scaling methods.
whatToWatch: Whether the approach is adopted by a lab or produces a released model
questions: Who authored the write-up, and has the approach been tested at scale?

stories.title: OpenAI case study: Ringg's voice AI agents resolve up to 65% of customer calls
stories.summary: OpenAI published a customer story saying Ringg's AI agents, built on its models, resolve as much as 65% of customer service calls without a human. The figure comes from an OpenAI-published case study, so it reflects the vendor's own framing. It is another example of OpenAI promoting enterprise voice-agent deployments on its platform.
stories.whyItMatters: Call-center automation is one of the clearest near-term revenue paths for AI agents, and figures like this shape enterprise buying decisions.
whatToWatch: Independent verification of resolution rates outside OpenAI's own case studies
Whether competitors publish comparable figures
questions: What counts as a 'resolved' call in this figure, and how was it measured?

sources.title: Ringg’s AI agents resolve up to 65% of customer calls with OpenAI

stories.title: Meta Connect 2026 recap: Muse glasses, voice and video features, and Charm
stories.summary: Meta's Connect 2026 conference covered new Muse smart glasses, plus voice and video features and a product called Charm, according to a Latent Space recap. The source is a summary roundup, so details beyond these names are not confirmed here. The event continues Meta's push to build AI deeper into its hardware and social products.
stories.whyItMatters: Meta's hardware and AI assistant strategy is a major bet on where consumer AI interaction moves next, beyond the chat interface.
whatToWatch: Pricing and availability details for Muse glasses
How Charm is positioned against rival AI assistants
questions: What exactly is Charm, and when do these features ship to consumers?

stories.title: Mercury 2.5 language model hits 770 tokens per second in benchmarks
stories.summary: Artificial Analysis benchmarked a model called Mercury 2.5 running at up to 770 tokens per second, a speed figure highlighted on Hacker News. The source does not name Mercury 2.5's developer or give pricing and quality comparisons alongside the speed number. Fast inference like this matters most for interactive and agentic workloads with heavy token use.
stories.whyItMatters: Inference speed increasingly competes with raw quality as a selling point, especially for real-time and agent workloads.
whatToWatch: Independent benchmarks comparing Mercury 2.5's quality against its speed
Pricing details from its developer
questions: Who develops Mercury 2.5, and how does its output quality compare to slower models?

stories.title: Report: federal officials label AI critics as 'foreign agents'
stories.summary: A report circulating on Hacker News says federal officials are targeting critics of the AI industry by labeling them foreign agents. The claim comes from independent journalist Ken Klippenstein's reporting. The source gives no further detail on which agency or which critics are named.
stories.whyItMatters: Using foreign-agent designations against AI critics would raise serious questions about free speech and the government's ties to industry.
whatToWatch: Official confirmation or denial from named agencies
Response from AI policy and civil liberties groups
questions: Which specific people or organizations are being targeted, and under what legal authority?
